NBA Expected Field-Goal Percentage — a SEMMA Project¶

Author: <your name> · Course: CMPE 255 · Repo: MeronDT/CMPE-255-Data-Mining-process · App: <deployed URL>

Data: NBA shot-chart detail (stats.nba.com), compiled by shufinskiy/nba_data (Apache-2.0; also on Kaggle). Every regular-season field-goal attempt with court coordinates, shot type, game clock and outcome. Population: five seasons, 2019-20 → 2023-24 (1,031,740 shots). Out-of-time check: 2024-25 (219,527 shots).

SEMMA (SAS Institute) organises the technical core of data mining into five steps. Each step below maps to the SAS Enterprise Miner nodes that implement it, so the same flow can be rebuilt in SAS (see the appendix).

Step Purpose Enterprise Miner nodes used here
Sample draw a representative, manageable sample; partition it Input Data · Sample · Data Partition
Explore understand distributions, relationships, anomalies StatExplore · MultiPlot / Graph Explore · Variable Selection · Cluster
Modify create, select, transform variables Drop · Transform Variables · Replacement · Interactive Binning · Impute
Model fit competing predictive models Regression · Decision Tree · Neural Network · Gradient Boosting · Ensemble
Assess compare models, check reliability, score new data Model Comparison · Cutoff · Score · Segment Profile

Headline result: a gradient-boosting model that estimates the make probability of any shot from where and how it is taken. It beats the zone-average baseline on every partition and on the unseen 2024-25 season, and is calibrated to within 0.9 percentage points in every decile. Comparing players' actual FG% with the xFG% of their shots separates shot making from shot selection, and that skill is repeatable (r = 0.68 across seasons).

How to run: Runtime → Run all (≈ 3–5 min on free Colab). Every figure, table, the model and the app are written to artifacts/.

Project context (pre-SEMMA)¶

SEMMA assumes the problem is already defined — unlike CRISP-DM it has no Business Understanding phase — so the problem is stated briefly here, to justify later choices.

  • Question: given where and how a shot is taken (location, shot type, game clock), what is the probability it goes in? This is expected field-goal percentage (xFG%) — a measure of shot quality, independent of who shoots.
  • Why it matters: raw FG% mixes two things: which shots a player takes and how well he makes them. A center who only dunks has a high FG% without being a great shooter. Comparing actual FG% with the xFG% of the same shots separates shot selection from shot making — the same idea as moving from box-score stats to advanced metrics when judging MVP candidates.
  • Target: SHOT_MADE_FLAG (1 = made). Unit: one field-goal attempt.
  • Success criteria: the champion model must (1) beat a zone-average baseline (league FG% for the shot's official court zone) in validation log loss, (2) be calibrated (predicted ≈ actual within each probability band), and (3) hold its performance on the unseen 2024-25 season.

# ============================ CONFIGURATION ============================
URL_TEMPLATE = "https://github.com/shufinskiy/nba_data/raw/main/datasets/shotdetail_{season}.tar.xz"
POPULATION_SEASONS = [2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023]   # file year = season start (2023 -> 2023-24)
OUT_OF_TIME_SEASON = 2024                              # 2024-25, scored only in Assess
TARGET       = "SHOT_MADE_FLAG"
SAMPLE_SIZE  = 200_000          # shots drawn from the population (justified by the learning curve in S.3)
PARTITION    = (0.6, 0.2, 0.2)  # train / validate / test, split by GAME so shots from one game stay together
RANDOM_STATE = 42
# =======================================================================

ART = Path("artifacts"); DATA, FIG, REP, MOD, APP = (ART / p for p in ("data", "figures", "reports", "model", "app"))
for p in (DATA, FIG, REP, MOD, APP):
    p.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

def savefig(name):
    plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig(FIG / f"{name}.png", dpi=120, bbox_inches="tight"); plt.show()

def draw_court(ax, color="#555", lw=1.2):
    """NBA half court in shot-chart units (tenths of feet, hoop at 0,0)."""
    from matplotlib.patches import Circle, Rectangle, Arc
    for p in [Circle((0, 0), 7.5, fill=False), Rectangle((-30, -7.5), 60, 0), Rectangle((-80, -47.5), 160, 190, fill=False),
              Arc((0, 142.5), 120, 120, theta1=0, theta2=180), Arc((0, 0), 80, 80, theta1=0, theta2=180),
              Rectangle((-220, -47.5), 0, 140), Rectangle((220, -47.5), 0, 140), Arc((0, 0), 475, 475, theta1=22, theta2=158),
              Rectangle((-250, -47.5), 500, 470, fill=False)]:
        p.set_edgecolor(color); p.set_linewidth(lw); ax.add_patch(p)
    ax.set_xlim(-250, 250); ax.set_ylim(-47.5, 422.5); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")

S — Sample¶

Goal: extract a portion of the data that is large enough to contain the significant information, yet small enough to process quickly — and partition it for honest model assessment.

S.1 Input Data¶

In [3]:
def load_season(season):
    path = DATA / f"shotdetail_{season}.csv"
    if not path.exists():                                  # download once, then reuse
        archive = DATA / f"shotdetail_{season}.tar.xz"
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(URL_TEMPLATE.format(season=season), archive)
        with tarfile.open(archive, "r:xz") as t:
            t.extractall(DATA)
        archive.unlink()
    d = pd.read_csv(path, dtype={c: "category" for c in ["GRID_TYPE", "PLAYER_NAME", "TEAM_NAME", "EVENT_TYPE", "ACTION_TYPE",
                                                         "SHOT_TYPE", "SHOT_ZONE_BASIC", "SHOT_ZONE_AREA", "SHOT_ZONE_RANGE", "HTM", "VTM"]})
    d.insert(0, "SEASON", f"{season}-{str(season + 1)[-2:]}")
    return d

t0 = time.time()
population = pd.concat([load_season(s) for s in POPULATION_SEASONS], ignore_index=True)
for c in population.select_dtypes("object").columns:
    population[c] = population[c].astype("category")
print(f"Population: {len(population):,} shots x {population.shape[1]} columns, {population['GAME_ID'].nunique():,} games "
      f"({time.time() - t0:.0f}s, {population.memory_usage(deep=True).sum() / 1e6:.0f} MB)")
display(population.groupby("SEASON", observed=True).agg(shots=(TARGET, "size"), games=("GAME_ID", "nunique"), fg_pct=(TARGET, "mean")).round(3))
population.head(3)

The 2019-20 (COVID suspension and bubble) and 2020-21 (72-game) seasons have fewer games, but shooting barely differs between seasons (FG% 46.0–47.5 %), so pooling all five seasons is reasonable. Rising FG% in 2022-23 and 2023-24 is worth remembering for the out-of-time test.

S.2 Sample¶

In [4]:
# Proportional stratified sample: preserves each season's share and its make/miss mix
frac = SAMPLE_SIZE / len(population)
sample = (population.groupby(["SEASON", TARGET], observed=True, group_keys=False)
                    .sample(frac=frac, random_state=RANDOM_STATE).reset_index(drop=True))

from scipy.stats import ks_2samp
check = pd.DataFrame({
    "population": [len(population), population[TARGET].mean(), population["SHOT_DISTANCE"].mean(),
                   (population["SHOT_TYPE"] == "3PT Field Goal").mean(), population["PERIOD"].gt(4).mean()],
    "sample": [len(sample), sample[TARGET].mean(), sample["SHOT_DISTANCE"].mean(),
               (sample["SHOT_TYPE"] == "3PT Field Goal").mean(), sample["PERIOD"].gt(4).mean()]},
    index=["shots", "FG%", "mean distance (ft)", "3PT share", "overtime share"]).round(4)
check["KS p-value"] = ["", "", round(ks_2samp(population["SHOT_DISTANCE"], sample["SHOT_DISTANCE"]).pvalue, 3),
                       "", ""]
check.to_csv(REP / "sample_representativeness.csv"); display(check)
population sample KS p-value
shots 1.031740e+06 199999.0000
FG% 4.677000e-01 0.4677
mean distance (ft) 1.356870e+01 13.5769 0.999
3PT share 3.917000e-01 0.3926
overtime share 6.000000e-03 0.0059

Representativeness. The 200k-shot sample (19 % of the population) reproduces the population almost exactly: FG% 46.77 % in both, mean distance 13.58 vs 13.57 ft, 3-point share 39.3 vs 39.2 %, overtime share 0.59 vs 0.60 %. The Kolmogorov–Smirnov test finds no difference in the shot-distance distribution (p = 0.999). Stratifying by season keeps each season's share; stratifying by outcome keeps the make rate exact. Because the sampling is proportional, the base rate is not distorted — important because the model must output real probabilities.

S.3 Data Partition¶

In [5]:
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupShuffleSplit

# Split by GAME_ID: shots from the same game never sit in two partitions (game-level effects can't leak)
tr_frac, va_frac, te_frac = PARTITION
idx_train, idx_rest = next(GroupShuffleSplit(1, test_size=va_frac + te_frac, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
                           .split(sample, groups=sample["GAME_ID"]))
rest = sample.iloc[idx_rest]
idx_val, idx_test = next(GroupShuffleSplit(1, test_size=te_frac / (va_frac + te_frac), random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
                         .split(rest, groups=rest["GAME_ID"]))
train, valid, test = sample.iloc[idx_train], rest.iloc[idx_val], rest.iloc[idx_test]
partitions = pd.DataFrame({p: {"shots": len(d), "games": d["GAME_ID"].nunique(), "FG%": round(d[TARGET].mean(), 4)}
                           for p, d in [("train", train), ("validate", valid), ("test", test)]}).T
partitions.to_csv(REP / "data_partition.csv"); display(partitions)
assert not (set(train.GAME_ID) & set(valid.GAME_ID)) and not (set(train.GAME_ID) & set(test.GAME_ID))

In [6]:
# Is SAMPLE_SIZE big enough? Learning curve: validation performance vs. training-set size
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, log_loss

quick = lambda d: d[["LOC_X", "LOC_Y", "PERIOD", "MINUTES_REMAINING", "SECONDS_REMAINING"]].assign(
    action=d["ACTION_TYPE"].cat.codes)
curve = []
for n in [2_000, 5_000, 10_000, 25_000, 50_000, len(train)]:
    sub = train.sample(n, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
    m = HistGradientBoostingClassifier(max_iter=150, random_state=RANDOM_STATE).fit(quick(sub), sub[TARGET])
    p = m.predict_proba(quick(valid))[:, 1]
    curve.append({"train_shots": n, "val_auc": roc_auc_score(valid[TARGET], p), "val_log_loss": log_loss(valid[TARGET], p)})
curve = pd.DataFrame(curve).round(4); curve.to_csv(REP / "learning_curve.csv", index=False); display(curve)
ax = curve.plot(x="train_shots", y="val_log_loss", marker="o", logx=True, legend=False, title="Learning curve (lower log loss = better)")
ax.set_ylabel("validation log loss"); savefig("sample_learning_curve")
train_shots val_auc val_log_loss
0 2000 0.6122 0.7398
1 5000 0.6251 0.6839
2 10000 0.6401 0.6583
3 25000 0.6573 0.6382
4 50000 0.6561 0.6378
5 120014 0.6622 0.6355

Is the sample big enough? Validation log loss drops quickly up to ~25k training shots (0.740 → 0.638) and then flattens (0.6378 at 50k, 0.6355 at 120k). Doubling the data beyond that buys almost nothing, so modeling on the full 1 M shots would cost time without adding information — SEMMA's core argument for sampling. (The curve uses a quick feature set because Modify comes later; it is indicative, and the margin is wide.)

Partitioning. Train/validate/test = 60/20/20 grouped by game (3,497 / 1,166 / 1,166 games), so shots from one game never sit in two partitions and game-level effects (pace, arena, opponent) cannot leak. FG% is 46.9 / 46.8 / 46.4 %.

Output of Sample: a stratified, representative 200k-shot sample; three game-grouped partitions; plus the full 2024-25 season held back for an out-of-time check in Assess.

Findings. EVENT_TYPE ("Made Shot"/"Missed Shot") matches the target perfectly (56,283 makes, 63,731 misses, zero disagreements) — it is the target in disguise and must be dropped. GRID_TYPE and SHOT_ATTEMPTED_FLAG are constant. There are no missing values in any column. Shots cluster at the rim (30 % in the restricted area) and beyond the arc (39 % threes); Jump Shot alone is 32 % of attempts.

E.3 Variable Selection (variable worth)¶

In [11]:
from sklearn.feature_selection import mutual_info_classif
cand = train.drop(columns=[TARGET, "EVENT_TYPE", "GRID_TYPE", "SHOT_ATTEMPTED_FLAG", "GAME_ID", "GAME_EVENT_ID", "GAME_DATE"])
s = cand.sample(30_000, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
enc = s.apply(lambda c: c.cat.codes if hasattr(c, "cat") else c)
discrete = [hasattr(cand[c], "cat") or cand[c].nunique() < 20 for c in enc.columns]
worth = pd.Series(mutual_info_classif(enc, train.loc[s.index, TARGET], discrete_features=discrete, random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
                  index=enc.columns).sort_values()
worth.plot.barh(color="#4C72B0", title="Variable worth: mutual information with SHOT_MADE_FLAG"); savefig("explore_variable_worth")
worth.sort_values(ascending=False).round(5).to_csv(REP / "variable_worth.csv")

Variable worth. Shot type (ACTION_TYPE, MI 0.043) and distance (SHOT_DISTANCE 0.037, zones 0.030, LOC_Y 0.022) carry the most information. Shooter identity also carries information (PLAYER_NAME 0.022) but is excluded by design: this model measures shot quality; who made the shot is analysed afterwards (A.4) as shot making. Game-clock fields carry little on their own (SECONDS_REMAINING 0.004) but matter in a specific situation (end-of-quarter heaves, see E.2). Distance is represented several overlapping ways — Modify replaces them with one consistent geometry.

E.4 Cluster (shot-location segments)¶

In [12]:
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
km = KMeans(n_clusters=8, n_init=10, random_state=RANDOM_STATE).fit(train[["LOC_X", "LOC_Y"]])
seg = train.assign(cluster=km.labels_)
profile = seg.groupby("cluster")[TARGET].agg(attempts="size", fg_pct="mean").round(3)
profile["mean_distance_ft"] = seg.groupby("cluster")["SHOT_DISTANCE"].mean().round(1)
display(profile.sort_values("mean_distance_ft"))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 7)); h = seg[seg["LOC_Y"] < 400].sample(20_000, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)

for k, (x, y) in enumerate(km.cluster_centers_):
    ax.text(x, y, f"{profile.loc[k, 'fg_pct']:.0%}", ha="center", fontsize=11, weight="bold",
            bbox=dict(facecolor="white", alpha=.8, edgecolor="none"))

Exploration findings¶

# Finding (training partition) Implication for Modify / Model
1 FG% falls from 76 % at 0 ft to 43 % by 4–5 ft, stays flat (≈ 43 %) through mid-range, then drops to ≈ 36 % beyond the arc and 23 % at 30 ft strongly non-linear distance effect → distance bins for the regression; trees handle it natively
2 Corner threes go in more often than above-the-break threes (38.1 % vs 35.6 %) — they are 22 ft instead of 23.75 ft add a corner-three flag and a shot angle
3 Shot type matters as much as location: cutting layups 70 %, running layups 61 %, but plain layups only 48 % and jump shots 37 % keep ACTION_TYPE; pool rare types
4 Shots with ≤ 2 s left in a quarter go in only 29 % of the time vs ≈ 47 % with time on the clock add game-clock features and a "heave" flag
5 K-means on location finds one rim cluster (60 % FG, 2 ft), two mid-range clusters (42–44 %), two corner/short-three clusters (≈ 39 %) and three above-the-break clusters (35–37 %) confirms that angle, not only distance, separates shot quality
⚠ EVENT_TYPE duplicates the target; GRID_TYPE, SHOT_ATTEMPTED_FLAG constant drop

M.2 Transform Variables · Replacement · Interactive Binning — as score code¶

In [14]:
SCORE_CODE = r"""
# Score code for the NBA xFG% model: the Modify step, shared by the notebook and the app.
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

RAW_INPUTS = ["LOC_X", "LOC_Y", "ACTION_TYPE", "PERIOD", "MINUTES_REMAINING", "SECONDS_REMAINING"]
NUMERIC = ["dist_ft", "angle_deg", "abs_angle", "is_three", "is_corner_three", "secs_left_period",
           "PERIOD", "is_overtime", "clutch", "heave"]
CATEGORICAL = ["action", "distance_bin"]
BIN_EDGES = [-0.1, 4, 10, 16, 23.75, 30, 100]
BIN_LABELS = ["0-4 ft", "4-10 ft", "10-16 ft", "16-23.75 ft", "23.75-30 ft", "30+ ft"]


def engineer(raw):
    # Transform raw shot records (RAW_INPUTS) into model inputs. Stateless, so it is safe to reuse anywhere.
    d = pd.DataFrame(raw).copy()
    x, y = d["LOC_X"].astype(float), d["LOC_Y"].astype(float)       # tenths of feet, hoop at (0, 0)
    out = pd.DataFrame(index=d.index)
    out["dist_ft"] = np.hypot(x, y) / 10
    out["angle_deg"] = np.degrees(np.arctan2(x, y))                  # 0 = straight on, +/-90 = along the baseline
    out["abs_angle"] = out["angle_deg"].abs()
    corner = (x.abs() >= 220) & (y <= 92.5)
    out["is_corner_three"] = corner.astype(int)
    out["is_three"] = (corner | (np.hypot(x, y) >= 237.5)).astype(int)
    out["secs_left_period"] = d["MINUTES_REMAINING"].astype(int) * 60 + d["SECONDS_REMAINING"].astype(int)
    out["PERIOD"] = d["PERIOD"].astype(int)
    out["is_overtime"] = (out["PERIOD"] > 4).astype(int)
    out["clutch"] = ((out["PERIOD"] >= 4) & (out["secs_left_period"] <= 120)).astype(int)
    out["heave"] = ((out["secs_left_period"] <= 3) & (out["dist_ft"] >= 30)).astype(int)
    out["action"] = d["ACTION_TYPE"].astype(str)
    out["distance_bin"] = pd.cut(out["dist_ft"], BIN_EDGES, labels=BIN_LABELS).astype(str)
    return out[NUMERIC + CATEGORICAL]


class AveragedModel:
    # Ensemble node: averages the predicted probabilities of already-fitted pipelines.
    def __init__(self, models):
        self.models = models
        self.classes_ = np.array([0, 1])

    def predict_proba(self, X):
        p = np.mean([m.predict_proba(X)[:, 1] for m in self.models], axis=0)
        return np.column_stack([1 - p, p])

    def predict(self, X):
        return (self.predict_proba(X)[:, 1] >= 0.5).astype(int)
"""
(APP / "shot_features.py").write_text(SCORE_CODE.lstrip())
if str(APP) not in sys.path:
    sys.path.insert(0, str(APP))

M.3 Replacement & Impute (inside the model pipeline)¶

Rare action levels (< 0.5 % of training shots) are replaced by a pooled "infrequent" level; missing values (none in training, but possible in new data) are imputed — both learned from the training partition only, inside the pipeline.

In [16]:
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import FunctionTransformer, OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer

def make_prep():
    return ColumnTransformer([
        ("num", Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("scale", StandardScaler())]), NUMERIC),
        ("cat", Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="constant", fill_value="missing")),
                          ("replace_rare", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist", min_frequency=0.005, sparse_output=False))]), CATEGORICAL)])

prep_preview = make_prep().fit(engineer(train))
names = prep_preview.get_feature_names_out()
print(f"{len(names)} model inputs after Replacement/one-hot; pooled rare actions:",
      sorted(prep_preview.named_transformers_["cat"].named_steps["replace_rare"].infrequent_categories_[0])[:12], "...")
X_tr, X_va, X_te = (d[RAW_INPUTS] for d in (train, valid, test))
y_tr, y_va, y_te = (d[TARGET].to_numpy() for d in (train, valid, test))

M — Model¶

Goal: let the software search for a combination of inputs that reliably predicts the outcome. Several model families compete; the validation partition is used to tune and compare them (as Enterprise Miner does).

In [17]:
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import brier_score_loss, accuracy_score

pipe = lambda est: Pipeline([("modify", FunctionTransformer(engineer)), ("prep", make_prep()), ("model", est)])
def scores(y, p):
    return {"log_loss": log_loss(y, p), "brier": brier_score_loss(y, p), "roc_auc": roc_auc_score(y, p), "accuracy": accuracy_score(y, p >= .5)}

fitted, val_pred, fit_secs = {}, {}, {}

Baseline — zone average¶

In [18]:
# The naive analyst's model: every shot gets the league FG% of its official court zone (from training data)
zone_keys = ["SHOT_ZONE_BASIC", "SHOT_ZONE_AREA", "SHOT_ZONE_RANGE"]
zone_rate = train.groupby(zone_keys, observed=True)[TARGET].mean()
def zone_baseline(d):
    return d[zone_keys].astype(str).apply(tuple, axis=1).map({tuple(map(str, k)): v for k, v in zone_rate.items()}).fillna(train[TARGET].mean()).to_numpy()
val_pred["Zone average (baseline)"] = zone_baseline(valid)
print("Baseline validation:", {k: round(v, 4) for k, v in scores(y_va, val_pred["Zone average (baseline)"]).items()})

Model families in the competition¶

Node What it is Assumptions / strengths Settings
Zone average league FG% of the official zone no learning beyond the zone; the "analyst's" benchmark —
Regression logistic regression on scaled inputs + one-hot shot type and distance bins linear in log-odds — distance bins supply the non-linearity; fully interpretable (dunks +1.0 to +1.7 log-odds, tip layups −1.0) default L2, max_iter=2000
Decision Tree single CART tree captures interactions, easy to read; high variance depth tuned on validation: 8 (log loss 0.6399)
Neural Network MLP, 32-16 hidden units flexible smooth functions; needs scaled inputs early stopping (37 epochs)
Gradient Boosting histogram gradient-boosted trees strongest on tabular data; interactions + non-linearity tuned on validation over 4 settings: learning rate 0.05, 31 leaves, 165 iterations
Ensemble average of regression, NN and boosting probabilities reduces variance if the members disagree —

A — Assess¶

Goal: evaluate the usefulness and reliability of the findings — compare models, check calibration, confirm on untouched data, and score new data.

A.1 Model Comparison (validation partition)¶

In [24]:

Gradient Boosting 0.6346 0.2229 0.6646 0.6355 3.9
Ensemble 0.6352 0.2232 0.6644 0.6367 NaN
Neural Network 0.6376 0.2242 0.6579 0.6329 11.1
Decision Tree 0.6399 0.2251 0.6575 0.6310 NaN

Zone average (baseline) 0.6572 0.2324 0.6341 0.6274 NaN 
Champion (lowest validation log loss): Gradient Boosting | beats zone baseline: True

Why log loss? xFG% is used as a probability (expected points = xFG% × shot value), so the selection criterion must reward accurate probabilities — not just ranking (AUC) or a 50 % cutoff (accuracy). Brier score agrees with log loss on the ranking of every model.

Result. Gradient boosting wins (log loss 0.6346), narrowly ahead of the ensemble (0.6352) and the neural network (0.6376). Every learned model beats the zone baseline (0.6572) — a 3.4 % reduction in log loss and AUC 0.665 vs 0.634. The gain looks modest because most of a shot's outcome is genuinely random once you know only where and what it was; the model cannot see the defender, the shooter's balance or the pass. All models are well calibrated on validation, and the champion's cumulative lift chart shows its top-rated 10 % of shots go in ≈ 1.8× as often as average.

In [25]:
from sklearn.metrics import RocCurveDisplay
from sklearn.calibration import calibration_curve
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(18, 5))
for m, p in val_pred.items():
    RocCurveDisplay.from_predictions(y_va, p, ax=axes[0], name=m)
    frac_pos, mean_pred = calibration_curve(y_va, p, n_bins=12, strategy="quantile")
    axes[1].plot(mean_pred, frac_pos, marker="o", ms=3, label=m)
axes[0].set_title("ROC — validation"); axes[1].plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "k--", lw=1)
axes[1].set(title="Calibration — validation", xlabel="predicted xFG%", ylabel="actual FG%"); axes[1].legend(fontsize=8)

# Cumulative lift chart (Enterprise Miner's standard assessment plot)
order = np.argsort(-val_pred[CHAMPION]); base = y_va.mean()
deciles = np.array_split(y_va[order], 10)
cum_lift = np.cumsum([d.sum() for d in deciles]) / np.cumsum([len(d) for d in deciles]) / base
axes[2].plot(range(10, 101, 10), cum_lift, marker="o"); axes[2].axhline(1, c="gray", ls="--")
axes[2].set(title=f"Cumulative lift — {CHAMPION}", xlabel="% of shots (sorted by xFG%)", ylabel="lift")
savefig("assess_model_comparison")

final_table = pd.DataFrame({k: {**scores(y, p), "baseline_log_loss": log_loss(y, b), "mean_xFG": p.mean(), "actual_FG": y.mean()}
                            for k, (y, p, b) in final.items()}).T.round(4)
final_table.to_csv(REP / "assess_final_performance.csv"); display(final_table)

In [28]:
# Critique fix: calibration by decile on the unseen 2024-25 season (not only on average)
y_oot, p_oot = final[list(final)[-1]][:2]
cal = pd.DataFrame({"xFG": p_oot, "made": y_oot})
cal["decile"] = pd.qcut(cal["xFG"], 10, labels=[f"D{i}" for i in range(1, 11)])
cal = cal.groupby("decile", observed=True).agg(shots=("made", "size"), mean_xFG=("xFG", "mean"), actual_FG=("made", "mean"))
cal["gap_pct_points"] = (cal["actual_FG"] - cal["mean_xFG"]) * 100
cal = cal.round(3); cal.to_csv(REP / "calibration_by_decile_2024_25.csv"); display(cal)
print(f"Largest decile gap: {cal['gap_pct_points'].abs().max():.1f} percentage points")

No over-fitting, and it travels to a new season. Test log loss (0.6345) equals validation (0.6346), so choosing the champion on validation did not over-fit. On the full 2024-25 season, which the model never saw, log loss is 0.6377 (baseline 0.6577) and AUC 0.657 — a small, expected decline. Calibration-in-the-large is excellent: predicted 46.4 % vs actual 46.7 %, and by decile every gap is ≤ 0.9 percentage points (from 30.5 % predicted / 31.0 % actual in the lowest decile to 83.7 % / 84.6 % in the highest). The three success criteria are met.

# Critique fix: is "shot making over expected" a repeatable skill or noise? Compare with the previous season.
prev = population[population["SEASON"] == "2023-24"]
prev = prev.assign(xFG=fitted[CHAMPION].predict_proba(prev[RAW_INPUTS])[:, 1])
prev_players = prev.groupby("PLAYER_NAME", observed=True).agg(FGA=(TARGET, "size"), FG=(TARGET, "mean"), xFG=("xFG", "mean"))
prev_players = prev_players[prev_players["FGA"] >= 500]
prev_players.index = prev_players.index.astype(str)
both = (players[["FG_over_expected"]].set_axis(players.index.astype(str))
        .join((prev_players["FG"] - prev_players["xFG"]).rename("FG_over_expected_2023_24"), how="inner"))
r = both.corr().iloc[0, 1]
both.to_csv(REP / "shot_making_persistence.csv")
print(f"{len(both)} players with 500+ FGA in both seasons; season-to-season correlation of FG over expected: r = {r:.2f}")
ax = both.plot.scatter("FG_over_expected_2023_24", "FG_over_expected", alpha=.6, title=f"Shot making persists across seasons (r = {r:.2f})")
ax.axhline(0, c="gray", lw=.8); ax.axvline(0, c="gray", lw=.8); savefig("assess_shot_making_persistence")

124 players with 500+ FGA in both seasons; season-to-season correlation of FG over expected: r = 0.68

Reading the chart: above the diagonal = the player makes more than his shots would predict (shot making); further right = he takes higher-quality shots (shot selection).

  • Nikola Jokić leads by far: 57.6 % on shots worth 46.7 % — +323 points over expected in one season. His shots are not unusually easy; he simply converts them.
  • Kevin Durant (+228) and Shai Gilgeous-Alexander (+197) take harder shots than Jokić (xFG 43.6 % and 46.1 % vs 46.7 %) and still make them — the profile of elite scorers.
  • Stephen Curry's xFG% is low (40.4 %) because of his shot diet (long threes), yet he is +143: raw FG% (44.8 %) badly undersells him.
  • At the bottom are mostly young players (Stephon Castle, Alex Sarr, Bilal Coulibaly; −107 to −138 points), consistent with shooting development curves.

Is this a skill or noise? For 124 players with 500+ attempts in both 2023-24 and 2024-25, FG over expected correlates r = 0.68 across seasons — it is largely repeatable. (2023-24 xFG is partly in-sample, about 12 % of those shots were training data, which slightly flatters that season.)

What the model does not know: defender distance, catch-and-shoot vs off-the-dribble beyond the ACTION_TYPE label, fatigue, and play context. Player-tracking data would close much of that gap, but it is not public.

SAS Enterprise Miner is available through SAS OnDemand for Academics when your professor registers the class (SAS Studio alone is free to individuals but has no Enterprise Miner). The cell below exports the exact modeling sample, so the SAS flow uses the same data.

Rebuild the flow in Enterprise Miner:

  1. New project → create a library → File Import node with nba_shots_sample_for_sas.csv.
  2. Input Data / variable roles: SHOT_MADE_FLAG = Target (binary); EVENT_TYPE, IDs, names, dates, SEASON = Rejected (same reasons as M.1); engineered columns = Input.
  3. Sample: Data Partition node — 60/20/20 (EM partitions rows randomly; note the difference from the game-grouped split here).
  4. Explore: StatExplore, MultiPlot, Variable Selection, Cluster (on LOC_X, LOC_Y).
  5. Modify: Replacement (rare action levels), Transform Variables (e.g. log of dist_ft), Impute.
  6. Model: Regression, Decision Tree, Neural Network, Gradient Boosting → Ensemble.
  7. Assess: Model Comparison (selection statistic: validation misclassification or average squared error ≈ Brier), then Score on the 2024-25 season.
  8. Report: screenshot the diagram and the Model Comparison results; compare them with section A.1 in your article.

Submission checklist¶

  • Analysis written for every step (author/course/URLs still to add in the header)
  • Critic round 1 done for all five steps (critiques/round_1.md) — rounds 2–3 to run in a fresh Claude chat
  • Run all completes without errors (≈ 80 s here; ≈ 3–5 min on free Colab)
  • artifacts/ committed (figures, reports, model, app) — artifacts/data/ ignored
  • App deployed; URL in the header and README
  • SAS Enterprise Miner demo (if the class is registered) with screenshots
  • Medium article published + YouTube walkthrough linked
